messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I have a binary response Y~Bernouilli(p) where logit(p) = -0.5 + X + U,  and U ~ Norm(0, .5 * (I  ⊗ phi )). I generate my response using:

N_fam <- 50; n_person <- 22 ; n_total <- N_fam * n_person
phi <- as.matrix(read.table("phi_mat_n22"))
phi_inv <- solve(phi) #22x22 matrix
X <- rbinom(n_total, 1, .5)
U <- c(t(rmvnorm(N_fam, sigma = .5 * phi))) # Same as c(inla.qsample(n= N_fam, Q = 2 * phi_inv))
Y <- rbinom(n_total, size = 1, prob = plogis(-0.5 + X * 1 + U))

In INLA, I am using the "generic0" latent model and using PC prior for hyperparameter with U=1 and alpha=0.01.

Prec <- Diagonal(N_fam) %x% phi_inv
fam_data = list(Y=Y, X=X, idu = 1:n_total)

formula <- Y ~ 1 + X + f(idu, model="generic0", Cmatrix=Prec, hyper = list(prec = list(prior = "pc.prec", param = c(1, .01)))
result <- inla(formula, data = fam_data, family = "binomial", Ntrials = rep(1, n_total), control.inla = list(correct = T, correct.factor = 10))

I looked at the coverage rate for the true precision (=2) across 500-1000 replicates (i.e. if it was between the 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles of the posterior distribution) for a given sample size. The coverage rate was 47% (SE 1.6%) for a sample of n=1100 and decreased to 35% (SE 1.5%) for a sample of  n=2200 and to 7.4% (SE 1%) for a sample of n= 5500 and to 0.4% (SE .3%) for a sample of n=11000.
I get that most of the time the true value isn't within the credible interval, and that gets worse as I increase the sample size. I understand that there is no replication in the data which will make it harder to get good estimates and that as I increase n I have more random effects being added, but I think I should get better estimates as I generate more data... Any help as to what may be going on?

I included the covariance matrix phi I use to generate the data within my family clusters.

Thank you!
Joelle

messages.body_plain:
As a sanity check, try a Gaussian response. Binary responses are often
the cause of problems (e-g- the Hauck-Donner effect), so you should
check to see if that's the problem. You could also try a binomial
response with a larger number of trials.

I haven't looked at the matrix, but this could be an issue of
sparseness §4.4.5 of McCullagh & Nelder): you only have one trial per
individual, so if the signal isn't too strong you can't estimate any
overdispersion. I'm not sure why the coverage is getting worse as the
sample size increases: I haven't looked at the pc prior in any detail
so I don't understand how it behaves.

I hope this helps, despite a certain amount of arm-waving.

Bob

> Dear INLA group,
>
> I wish to use INLA package to carry out an anlysis using informative
> priors on fixed effects.
> The objective is to use previous sample results (historical data) to
> form prior distributions included in subsequent sample analyses.
> An good example is https://support.sas.com/rnd/app/examples/stat/Baye

>

>

Yes. this is available with the options 'weights', like

inla(..., weights = w)

set it do the 'scale parameter' a_0 (in the SAS reference) for the old
data, and to 1 for new data.

as you'll see, you have enable this option before using it (every
time).

H

          log-likelihood[i] is changed into
          weights[i]*log-likelihood[i]. Default value is rep(1,
          n.data). Due to the danger of mis-interpreting the results
          (see below), this option is DISABLED by default. You can
          enable this option for the rest of your ‘R’ session, doing
          ‘inla.setOption(enable.inla.argument.weights=TRUE)’. WARNING:
          The normalizing constant for the likelihood is NOT
          recomputed, so ALL marginals (and the marginal likelihood)
          must be interpreted with great care. Possibly, you may want
          to set the prior for the hyperparameters to ‘"uniform"’ and
          the integration strategy to ‘"eb"’ to mimic a
          maximum-likelihood approach.

if this is about transforming hyperparameters, then *always* start from
the marginals on the internal scale. they are constructed to be
Gaussian like and well behaved. although the marginal you put it, is
interpolated (using inla.smarginal), there are cases where you can
loose accuracy mapping between different parametersisations.

in general 'si' would be more accurate than 's1' but not in this case.

r$internal.marginals.hyperpar

> r = inla(y ~ 1, data = data.frame(y=0))

> mi = r$internal.marginals.hyperpar[[1]]
> s1 = inla.tmarginal(function(x) 1/sqrt(x), m1)

> plot(s1)
> lines(si)

ohh, that was quite a difference. Intuitively, I would bet on A, as one
avoid the transformation. since exp(x) is kind of exploding, then
you're right, the tail behaviour would dominate here. Also I would
check that the density does indeed goes to zero. in the function
'inla.smarginal' you can also extrapolate, but it do that at linear
rate in log-scale. unfortunately, the tail behaviour might not be so
accurate, in the sense that the rate is postulated not necessarily
computed.

In general, I am a bit (or even more than a bit) sceptical to E()
values when tail dominate, like the E(precision) is often meaningless
due to the tail, which in fact boil down to that squared error does not
make sense. E(log(prec)) is usually much much better. (its like why
should be care of an unbiased estimator for variance? the distribution
is skewed hence I do not care about E(variance)?)

Maybe I would consider to use quantiles instead, f.ex  median. from the
marginal you can get the median, and then exp(median) is the median in
the new scale. much less mess and hopefully more stable with less tail
influence.

H

  covariate.ppy.g <- inla.group(c(covariate.pp, covariate.y))

                                        covariate.pp=covariate.ppy.g[1:(nv+n.c)])))

                                       covariate.y=covariate.ppy.g[nv+1:n.c])))

On Wed, 2016-03-23 at 19:40 -0700, Yimer Wasihun wrote:
>
> My work is on spatiotemporal modeling of geostatistical spatiotemporal data using SPDE approach. Let me show part of my code and I will proceed with the questions,
> Formula <- y ~ -1 + Intercept + f(field, model=spde, group=field.group, diagonal=1e-06,
>           control.group=list(model="rw1", scale.model=TRUE, adjust.for.con.comp=TRUE))
>
> In previous discussions, it has been mentioned that for intrinsic models (which are almost singular) we need to specify constr=TRUE and add diagonal=1e-06 by default (and very small values in general) to make them non-singular.
>
> Q1) Is the above formula correct for specifying the diagonal value to be added on the precision matrix of rw1?

Hi,

this is correct, although do you not need 'adjust.for.con.comp' as it is not used (its only for
model = besag).

Formula <- y ~ -1 + Intercept + f(field, model=spde, group=field.group, diagonal=1e-06,
          control.group=list(model="rw1", scale.model=TRUE, adjust.for.con.comp=TRUE))

and it is not clear if you really need 'diagonal=', or if you want the constr=F|T.

The 'diagonal' term is automatically added when you specify an intrinsic model, like 'rw2', for which also constr=T is default.
This to avoid confounding with the intercept. Also, due to how the 'constr=T' is handled internally, ie the algorithm used to compute it,
then the model has to be proper BEFORE the constr=T is accounted for. So we deal with this by adding a small term on the diagonal.

In your case, then the 'spde' model is likely already proper, hence you do not need diagonal=, unless you experience
numerical instabilities.

be aware, that the group model rw1, is intrinsic, which normally, in this setting does not create trouble, as the level for each
location is determined by data, hence the 'time' defined by 'group' is proper. if you experience trouble here (read HUGE stderrors),
then you may revisit this issue.

I would guess that you can remove 'diagonal' and 'adjust.for.con.comp'.

> Q2) When we use rw1 or rw2 model under control.group,  how is it possible to include the constr=TRUE option in r-inla?

yes, if you have

f(space, group = time, constr=T)

this means that the (weighted) sum over space is zero, for every timepoint.  so this is replicated to |time| constraints.

>
> Using the above formula, I tried to use diagonal=1e-06, diagonal=1e-05, diagonal=1e-04 and diagonal=1e-03 , and the spatial predictions are not the same for all these diagonal values.  So, I am afraid if this is because the diagonal values have been misplaced, and constr=TRUE option wasn't included.

try to set it to zero, which should be the correct option.   if you run into trouble, let me know

Best,

The precision for this space-time model is the Kronecker product between the precision matrix from the SPDE model and the structure matrix defined by the temporal neighbourhood, Q (x) R, and has rank deficiency equals the number of nodes in the mesh.

The diagonal added (in the way Håvard Rue <https://www.ntnu.edu/employees/havard.rue> described) is enough to make the model proper, however, as he warned, you may see HUGE standard errors.

The sum-to-zero constraints, see [1] and [2], is the usual way to solve this problem. In this case the number of such constraints is equal to the number of mesh nodes, as it needs sum-to-zero constraint for each time series. Since the computational time grows squared on the number of such constraints, it is not a cheap solution. The use of 'ar1' model is computationally convenient.

Elias
